newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Boeing says U.S. merger probe to end in June.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Boeing says U.S. merger probe to end in June.

text.p: Boeing Co's vice-president for European affairs Jim Frank said on Wednesday he expected that the United States Federal Trade Commission would complete the review of its merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp by the end of June or early July.
"The latest I have heard is that the U.S. authority is trying to complete their assessment towards the end of June, early July," Frank told Reuters.

If this is confirmed, it clearly indicates that the FTC intends to take the lead in the investigation of the mega-merger between the two aircraft manufacturers about which the European Commission has raised strong doubts.
It was originally expected that the United States would complete its assessment after the Commission had taken a decision, which must happen by July 31.
European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert in the meantime dismissed press reports that the merger could trigger a transatlatic trade war.

"Van Miert discards those rumours or comments about a potential trade war as, I quote, totally nonsensical," his spokesman, Willy Helin, told the Commission's daily news briefing in reply to questions.
Helin said it was wrong to envisage castratrophe scenarios so early in the merger review and that negotiations had still to take place.
"We still hope that after they get the statement of objections, the parties involved will come up with remedies which will allow us to hopefully clear the file. But we are not there yet", Helin said.
Frank, concerned about avoiding any inflamatory statements, also expressed hope that any differences would be ironed out.
"I don't know what (the Commission's) concerns are but I'm not saying that I'm opposed to sitting down to discuss those concerns with them," he said.
The Commission is expected to detail its grievances in a so-called statement of objections before the end of the month.

Boeing says the Commission's merger task force, which prepares decisions for the full Commission, does not have the authority to impose any changes on the merger with McDonnell Douglas, arguing that it should let the FTC take the lead.
"In this case we are expecting that the FTC is the one who takes the lead role, that whatever they are suggesting will be accepted as reasonable by the merger task force," Frank said.

Under EU rules, the Commission has the power to review all mergers and acquisitions involving companies making more than 250 million European currency units each in sales in the 15-nation market and with a combined global turnover of five billion Ecus.
It can ultimately block the deal if it thinks it will harm fair competition in the EU and no remedies are provided.
Boeing and McDonnell Douglas are projected to have 1997 sales of $48 billion together.

The merger would make the new company, which would operate under the Boeing name, the world's largest aerospace company ahead of Airbus Industrie, the consortium made up of aircraft manufacturers in France, Britain, Germany and Spain.
But Frank denied the deal would give Boeing a dominant position, let alone strengthen it -- something the Commission seems to have few doubts about.
"I contest the point that we have a dominant position which would be made stronger," he said.

The situation in the last few years showed that Boeing has about 60 percent of the world's commercial aviation market, with Airbus holding between 30 and 35 percent and McDonnell only three percent, Frank said.
